GitHub Copilot review

The safest default choice for most developers, thanks to how deeply it integrates with existing tools.

Pros

  • Deep IDE integration
  • Strong autocomplete quality
  • Free tier is genuinely usable for small projects

Cons

  • Chat features lag behind some competitors

Real use cases

Inline code autocomplete Suggests whole lines or functions as you type, in your existing IDE.
Boilerplate and test generation Speeds up repetitive scaffolding and unit test writing.
Learning a new codebase Chat features help explain unfamiliar code, though less deeply than dedicated coding assistants.

Bottom line

Copilot's advantage isn't raw model quality — it's distribution. It's already inside the editor most developers use, with autocomplete good enough that most people never think to look elsewhere for day-to-day coding. The chat/reasoning side is a step behind specialized coding assistants, so power users pairing on complex refactors may want a second tool alongside it.

Frequently asked questions

Is GitHub Copilot free?

There's a limited free tier; full access starts at roughly $10/mo for individuals.

Which IDEs does Copilot support?

VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, Neovim, and others via official extensions.

Does Copilot have a chat mode?

Yes, though its reasoning depth lags behind some dedicated coding assistants on complex tasks.

Is Copilot good for students?

GitHub has offered free access to verified students in the past — check current eligibility on GitHub's site.

Does Copilot have an API?

No public API for the coding assistant itself.

When was GitHub Copilot last tested by Luvent?

We last tested it on 2026-07-10.
